newsitem.title: HONG KONG: S&P consultancy sees pros, cons for Asia in EMU.
newsitem.headline: S&P consultancy sees pros, cons for Asia in EMU.

text.p: European Monetary Union (EMU) is likely to have both positive and negative effects on Asia, Standard and Poor's economic consultancy group MMS International said on Tuesday.
"The implications for Asia are mixed, as Asia is likely to see both positives and negatives from the EMU process," Callum Henderson, managing analyst at MMS Hong Kong, told a seminar.

He said the most obvious positive is that the creation of the Euro, the single European currency, will put a greater emphasis on inter-Asian foreign exchange activities as traders seek opportunities outside Europe.
This will come "just at a time when inter-Asian physical trade is taking an ever-increasing amount of the total trade in the region," Henderson said.
Uncertainty about European markets in the run-up to EMU could benefit Asia as investors shift assets away from Europe.
Once the EMU becomes a reality, Asian business is likely to benefit from reduced hedging costs and lower currency risks.
In the longer-term, however, a successful EMU could hurt Asia's competitiveness versus Europe, forcing accelerated restructuring of the region's markets, Henderson said.
The launch of the EMU is scheduled for January 1999, but MMS predicts a delay in the start-up date to give member countries more time to qualify.
"MMS expects a modest delay in the project to allow for growth and fiscal tightening to feed through and permit a broader group of member states to qualify," Henderson said.
"The only viable alternative is a very flexible interpretation of the criteria, whether for a core or broad grouping, and a weak Euro from the start," he said.
Very few European countries currently meet the economic criteria for full monetary union.
Germany and France, for example, do not meet the budget deficit requirements, which stipulate that each country's budget deficit must not exceed three percent of its gross domestic product (GDP).
The German government has vowed to keep its budget deficit below three percent of GDP but many economists are skeptical.
MMS forecasts a German budget deficit to GDP ratio of 3.3 percent for 1997.
If Germany, as one of the core countries, does not meet the target and the EMU nevertheless starts on time, the criteria would have been interpreted flexibly rather than strictly.

"At least in theory, this would make it difficult to exclude Italy and the Iberian states, particularly when these, together with other 'non-core' member states have the voting power to block the core grouping plan which is supported by Germany," said Henderson.
He said financial markets would not be unnerved by a short delay in the EMU if it was deemed necessary for stability.
